A_before_merge.title: When people won, the company sued the state
A_before_merge.summary:
When protests or governments ended a water or mining deal on this map, the foreign owners often took the country to arbitration. Most of these claims went to ICSID, the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, which its own website calls "one of the five organizations of the World Bank Group". The legal basis was usually a bilateral investment treaty, an agreement between two countries that lets a company from one sue the other.

In Cochabamba, Bolivia rescinded Aguas del Tunari's water contract in April 2000 after mass protests. The consortium, led by Bechtel with Abengoa, had moved its registration to Amsterdam in 1999, which let it use the Netherlands-Bolivia treaty (Democracy Center). It claimed $50 million at ICSID, half of it lost future profits (Earthjustice). On 19 January 2006 the companies dropped the case for a token 2 bolivianos, about 30 US cents; Bolivia had spent about $1 million on its defense (Democracy Center). In Dar es Salaam, Tanzania ended City Water's contract in May 2005, and Biwater Gauff sought $19 to 20 million (ASIL). In July 2008 the ICSID tribunal found Tanzania had breached the UK treaty but awarded nothing, because the losses came from the company's own failures (IISD). A separate contract tribunal had already ruled against City Water in December 2007 and awarded about £3 million to the Tanzanian water authority.

In Buenos Aires, Argentina rescinded Aguas Argentinas' concession in March 2006. Its owners Suez, Aguas de Barcelona and Vivendi (at ICSID) and AWG (under UNCITRAL rules, another arbitration system) claimed $1,019.2 million as of June 2008 and $868 million by the end, by the award's own record; press figures run higher, at $1.2 billion (Suez's statement) and more than $1.3 billion (Diario de Cuyo). In April 2015 the tribunal awarded $405 million in total, about $21 million of it to AWG (Freshfields; El Cronista). In April 2019 Suez said a discounted settlement brought it €220 million in cash. In Colombia, the state banned mining in the Santurbán páramo, a high wetland that supplies water to over 2.5 million people. Eco Oro claimed $690 million plus interest under the Canada-Colombia trade agreement (El Universal). The tribunal found in 2021 that part of the ban's handling breached the treaty; in July 2024 it awarded no damages (Latham & Watkins, Colombia's counsel).

Across these four treaty claims, companies asked for about $1.78 billion and were awarded $405 million, all in the Buenos Aires case. Of 10 cases on this map where protests, courts or governments stopped or ordered an end to a company's deal, four led to a filed treaty claim and one more, El Alto, to a formal treaty notice by Suez in May 2005. Related: in Manila, Maynilad itself tried to end its contract in 2002-2003 and lost an ICC contract arbitration that ordered it to pay 7 billion pesos; in Tucumán, Argentina (not on this map), Vivendi won $105 million at ICSID in 2007.
A_before_merge.implications: These cases show that ending a privatization does not end the dispute. The company can take the fight to an international tribunal, outside the country's courts, and claim lost future profits as well as money spent. Bolivia, Tanzania and Colombia spent years defending claims that ended with little or no money paid; Bolivia's defense alone cost about $1 million. Argentina paid, at a discount. Tribunals found treaty breaches in Tanzania and Colombia even where they awarded nothing. The record found here does not show whether any government kept or softened a contract for fear of a claim. ICSID is part of the World Bank Group, whose lending was tied to Cochabamba's privatization; in that case each side named one arbitrator and the World Bank's president named the presiding one (IPS).

countries.note: Aguas del Tunari claimed $50 million at ICSID after the April 2000 rescission and dropped the case in January 2006 for 2 bolivianos; Bolivia spent about $1 million defending it (Earthjustice, Democracy Center). Suez also sent a letter alleging a treaty breach over El Alto on 20 May 2005 (Spronk, bilaterals.org).

ICSID found in July 2008 that Tanzania breached the UK-Tanzania treaty, including by expropriation, but awarded Biwater Gauff no damages, against a $19-20 million claim; each side bore its own costs (ASIL, IISD).

The Buenos Aires tribunal awarded $405 million in April 2015 after the March 2006 rescission (Freshfields); Suez said in April 2019 that a settlement brought it €220 million in cash (Suez). Vivendi also won $105 million over Tucumán in 2007 (Vivendi).
Eco Oro claimed $690 million plus interest, about $1.1 billion; the July 2024 award granted no damages and did not order Colombia to pay costs (El Universal, Latham & Watkins).
An ICC tribunal ruled on 10 November 2003 that Maynilad had no grounds to end its Manila concession and must pay 7 billion pesos to the government for overdue fees (WWD).
Bechtel, based in San Francisco, led Aguas del Tunari. ICSID sits in Washington as part of the World Bank Group (ICSID).
Aguas del Tunari moved its residence to Amsterdam in 1999 to use the 1992 Netherlands-Bolivia treaty (Democracy Center).
Suez and Vivendi were ICSID claimants against Argentina; Vivendi also brought the Tucumán claim (Freshfields, Vivendi).
Abengoa was Bechtel's partner in Cochabamba; Aguas de Barcelona was a Buenos Aires claimant (Earthjustice, Freshfields).
Biwater sued Tanzania under the UK treaty; AWG won about $21 million against Argentina under UNCITRAL rules (ASIL, Global Arbitration News).
Eco Oro, a Canadian junior mining company, sued under the Canada-Colombia free trade agreement (Latham & Watkins, El Universal).

timeline.event: Vivendi and its Tucumán water company start a dispute with Argentina over the provincial water concession, later heard at ICSID.
Aguas del Tunari moves its residence to Amsterdam, gaining access to the Netherlands-Bolivia treaty.
Aguas del Tunari's claim against Bolivia is registered at ICSID (case ARB/02/3) after the April 2000 rescission.
An ICC tribunal rules on 10 November that Maynilad had no grounds to end its Manila concession and must pay 7 billion pesos.
On 20 May Suez writes to Bolivia accusing it of breaching the France-Bolivia treaty over El Alto, opening the six-month negotiation period the treaty requires before legal action.
The ICSID tribunal rules on 21 October that it has jurisdiction over Aguas del Tunari's claim.
Bechtel and Abengoa drop their $50 million claim against Bolivia on 19 January for a token 2 bolivianos.
In December a contract tribunal rejects City Water's claims and awards about £3 million to the Dar es Salaam water authority.
On 20 August an ICSID tribunal awards Vivendi and its Tucumán subsidiary $105 million plus interest and costs.
ICSID finds on 24 July that Tanzania breached its treaty with the UK but awards Biwater Gauff no damages.
The Buenos Aires tribunal finds Argentina liable and postpones the amount.
On 9 April the tribunal awards the former Aguas Argentinas owners $405 million in total.
Suez says a settlement with Argentina over the Buenos Aires award brought the Suez group €220 million in cash.
In September the Eco Oro tribunal finds Colombia's mining ban was not expropriation but that parts of its handling breached the treaty.
On 15 July the Eco Oro tribunal awards no damages, against a claim of about $690 million plus interest.
Eco Oro applies on 30 July to annul the damages award.

A_before_merge.uncertain: Claim amounts differ by source: Cochabamba is $25 million (IPS, 2002) or $50 million (Earthjustice, Democracy Center); Eco Oro is about $690 million principal or $1.1 billion with interest; Buenos Aires is $1,019.2 million as of June 2008 in the award, $1.2 billion in Suez's statement and 'more than $1.3 billion' in Diario de Cuyo, while IPS (2006) said Suez sought to recover $1.7 billion it had invested. Bechtel's stake in Aguas del Tunari is reported as controlling (Democracy Center) or 27.5% (IPS, 2002). Suez's own release says its €220 million covered the Buenos Aires award; a Buenos Aires Times report that tied it to the Santa Fe award is contradicted by that release. Whether and how AWG's $21 million was paid is not reported. No registered arbitration was found for El Alto after Suez's 2005 notice, and no claim was found for Conga, Jakarta, Canbalam, Santa Rita or Ban Chaung; a confidential claim cannot be ruled out. Eco Oro's annulment application, filed 30 July 2025, was pending as of the latest source found. Bolivia's defense in the Cochabamba case cost about $1 million (Democracy Center); legal costs for Tanzania and Colombia are not reported; Tanzania's tribunal left each side to bear its own costs, and Colombia's ordered no costs against Colombia.

B_before_merge.title: Investors sue the state after privatization
B_before_merge.summary:
Foreign companies that bought or ran privatized water, gas and power services used investment treaties to sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts or took services back. Most cases go to ICSID, the World Bank Group's arbitration centre in Washington. Two of the water deals were themselves tied to the World Bank: Bolivia's 1999 Cochabamba contract with Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari was part of a World Bank-backed privatization plan, and in Tanzania the World Bank and other lenders provided $140m in 2003 on condition that a private firm run the water and sewerage system, which went to Biwater's City Water in Dar es Salaam. Bolivia cancelled its contract after protests in April 2000; Tanzania ended Biwater's in May 2005 and deported its managers. Bechtel dropped its claim in a 2006 settlement; the Biwater tribunal found breaches but awarded $0 in damages (2008).

Argentina is the main target. After its 2001–2002 crisis, 46 treaty cases had been filed by March 2009 (Kluwer Arbitration Blog) and 50 between 2001 and 2012 (South Centre). Awards include CMS Gas $133.2m (2005), Azurix (an Enron water firm) $165.2m (2006), Enron $106.2m and Sempra $128.2m (2007, later annulled), BG Group $185.2m (2007), National Grid $54m (2008), Vivendi (Tucumán water) $105m (2007) and Suez and its partners $405m in total (2015; the owners' claim is reported as $1.2bn and more than $1.3bn in the press, and as $1,019.2m in June 2008 and $868m by the end in the award itself). After the US suspended Argentina's trade preferences in 2012 over unpaid Azurix and CMS awards, Argentina settled five awards worth $677m in October 2013 with bonds of $506m face value, after a 25% cut. Other tribunals rejected claims: Urbaser (Spain) got no damages in 2016, and Veolia's €174m claim over Alexandria's waste contract, partly over Egypt's minimum wage rise, was dismissed in 2018. Outside privatized services, Ecuador agreed to pay Occidental $980m (2016) and Vattenfall got €1.43bn from Germany (2021) over the nuclear phase-out.

countries.note: Aguas del Tunari (Bechtel subsidiary) won a 40-year Cochabamba water contract in 1999 under a World Bank-backed plan; Bolivia ended it in April 2000 after protests. Bechtel sued in 2001 under the Bolivia–Netherlands BIT and dropped the claim in a January 2006 settlement (bilaterals.org).

Biwater's City Water ran Dar es Salaam water from 2003 under a $140m project funded by the World Bank and others; Tanzania terminated it in May 2005. ICSID found four treaty breaches but awarded $0 damages (24 July 2008) (IISD).

Respondent in 46 treaty cases by March 2009 (Kluwer Arbitration Blog) and 50 in 2001–2012, 27 of 36 fully public ones aimed at post-crisis measures (South Centre 2015). About $1.4bn in fixed compensation across 15 cases.

Veolia Propreté claimed €174m under the France–Egypt treaty over its 2000 Alexandria waste contract, partly over a minimum wage rise; the ICSID tribunal's dismissal was reported in May 2018 (AFTINET via bilaterals.org).

Context, not a privatized service: Ecuador took Occidental's oil Block 15 in 2006; ICSID awarded $1.77bn in 2012, cut to about $1bn plus interest on annulment in 2015; Ecuador agreed to pay $980m (bilaterals.org, 2015–2016).
Context, not a privatization: Vattenfall claimed €4.7bn at ICSID under the Energy Charter Treaty over the nuclear phase-out; Germany settled in March 2021, paying Vattenfall €1.43bn (IISD).

US claimants against Argentina: CMS ($133.2m), Azurix ($165.2m), Enron ($106.2m), Sempra ($128.2m), LG&E ($57.4m), Continental Casualty ($2.8m) (Kluwer Arbitration Blog). Bechtel owned Aguas del Tunari (Bolivia).

Vivendi's subsidiary Aguas del Aconquija won $105m over Tucumán water in 2007 (Reuters via bilaterals.org); Vivendi was a co-claimant with Suez and AGBAR in the Buenos Aires water case; Suez and its co-claimants won $405m in total in 2015; Veolia sued Egypt.

Biwater Gauff (Tanzania), owned by English and German parents, sued under the UK–Tanzania BIT (IISD). BG Group won $185.2m (2007) and National Grid $54m (2008) against Argentina, both under UNCITRAL rules (Kluwer Arbitration Blog).
Urbaser and Consorcio de Aguas Bilbao Bizkaia sued Argentina under the Spain–Argentina BIT over Buenos Aires Province water (AGBA); the 8 Dec 2016 award found a breach but gave no damages (IISD).
Vattenfall, a Swedish-owned company, received €1.43bn from Germany in the March 2021 settlement (IISD).
Aguas del Tunari's claim against Bolivia was brought under the Bolivia–Netherlands bilateral investment treaty (bilaterals.org).

timeline.event: Vivendi's Tucumán subsidiary Aguas del Aconquija withdraws from its water concession, accusing the province of changing its terms.
Bolivia grants Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari a 40-year Cochabamba water contract under a World Bank-backed privatization plan; rates rise 100–200% for some.
After a general strike in January and protests in April, Bolivia terminates the Aguas del Tunari contract.
Biwater's City Water signs contracts in February to run Dar es Salaam water, under a $140m project funded by the World Bank and others on condition of private operation.
Tanzania terminates City Water's contract in May and deports its senior managers on 1 June.
CMS Gas Transmission is awarded $133.2m against Argentina on 12 May.
Bechtel drops its claim against Bolivia in a January settlement; Bolivia states the termination was due to civil unrest, not company acts.
An ICSID tribunal awards Azurix $165.2m against Argentina on 14 July.
Vivendi is awarded $105m over the Tucumán water concession in August.
On 24 July the Biwater tribunal finds Tanzania breached the UK treaty but awards no damages.
A Kluwer Arbitration Blog count lists 46 treaty cases against Argentina since 2001, with nothing yet paid on the awards.
The US suspends Argentina from its trade preference scheme over unpaid Azurix and Blue Ridge (CMS) awards.
An ICSID tribunal awards Occidental $1.77bn against Ecuador over the 2006 seizure of Block 15.
Argentina settles five awards worth $677m with bonds of $506m face value, after a 25% cut in principal.

On 9 April a tribunal orders Argentina to pay Suez and its partners $405m in total over Buenos Aires water; Suez's statement put the original claim at $1.2bn, while the award records $1,019.2m as of June 2008.
Ecuador agrees to pay Occidental $980m after an annulment committee cut the award.
On 8 December the Urbaser tribunal awards no damages and becomes the first to hear a human-rights counterclaim, on water, which it dismisses.
An ICSID tribunal's dismissal of Veolia's €174m claim against Egypt over the Alexandria waste contract is reported in May.
Germany settles the nuclear phase-out claims; Vattenfall receives €1.43bn of the €4.7bn it sought.

uncertain: The amount Bechtel's Aguas del Tunari claimed is given as $25m by bilaterals.org; other reports give different figures that were not checked here.

Whether Argentina's 2001–2002 emergency measures were lawful is contested: tribunals rejected Argentina's necessity defence in CMS, Enron, Sempra and BG but accepted the treaty exception in LG&E and Continental (South Centre 2015).
Total sums actually paid by Argentina across all crisis cases are not established here; the 2013 settlement covered five awards, and the South Centre gives about $900m in final rulings by 2015.
Veolia's claim against Egypt was dismissed but the reasons were not published at the time, so how the minimum-wage issue was decided is unknown.
The exact amount paid to each of the five 2013 claimants is not given in the pages read.

The Biwater claim amount was not confirmed in the pages checked. No source explains the gap between the press figures for the Buenos Aires claim ($1.2bn; more than $1.3bn) and the award's own figures.

B_px.implications: Investment treaties let foreign companies that bought or ran privatized services sue governments that froze tariffs, changed contracts or took services back, most often at ICSID, the World Bank Group's arbitration centre. Results vary: Argentina, the main target, faced awards such as $405m to Suez and its partners, while the Biwater tribunal awarded $0, Bechtel dropped its claim and Veolia's claim against Egypt was dismissed. Two of the water deals, in Bolivia and Tanzania, were themselves tied to the World Bank. Some Argentine awards were later annulled or settled for less, and the total Argentina actually paid is not established.

B_px.overlap: Yes, substantially, with company-sued-the-state: same mechanism and ICSID's World Bank tie, and the same Cochabamba, Dar es Salaam, Buenos Aires and Tucumán disputes. New here: the wider Argentine crisis claims and the 2013 bond settlement, Urbaser, Veolia, Occidental and Vattenfall. Both Buenos Aires claim figures are press figures for the same claim; the award records the four owners' total as $1,019.2m in June 2008 and $868m at the end. See r19f_pats_fixes.json.
